pages.body:
# Start here

TribeCode lets a few friends, or one person with AI helpers, build apps, games and websites together, and run the business around them. Each friend can bring their own AI (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor…). The work lives in your shared GitHub repo, and friends join with a link.

## The idea in one minute

- **Your tribe, your files.** Chat, docs and tasks are plain files in the tribe's folder; the code is saved to your own GitHub.
- **Friends join with a link**, on a phone or a computer.
- **People decide, agents do the work.** Your AI proposes; you approve with one tap.

## Your first two minutes

1. **Open the app.** Nothing is created for you. **Make it yours** asks for your name, icon, theme and language (skip any of it), then Flint offers a quick look around.
2. **On Home, tap Start your first project** (or **Join with a link**). It starts on this device; choose where it lives any time later.
3. **Invite a friend.** The invite sheet copies the link.
4. **Connect your AI** (optional). Flint works without one.

**See how TribeCode works** in the **?** menu runs a demo one step at a time and clears itself afterwards.

## Where things are

| You want to… | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| See the project at a glance | **Dashboard** |
| Talk | **Messages** |
| Notes and any file | **Files** |
| Design a screen, site, game or slides | **Design** (Flint beside the canvas; **Advanced** for layers) |
| See what needs doing | **Task Board** |
| Try what you built | **Preview** |
| See who's here and where | **People**, top right |
| See what the agents do | **Agents Hub** |
| Approve things | The **bell**, top right |
| Run a business, hire, learn, add tools | **Company**, **Work**, **Academy**, **Marketplace** ([guides](10-company-mode.md)) |
| Anything else | **Ctrl K** |

The circles on the far left are your projects. The flame logo takes you Home.

## Words you'll see

- **Tribe**: your group and everything it makes.
- **Project**: one thing you build. A tribe can have several.
- **Host**: the computer (or cloud) that keeps the tribe online.
- **Agent**: someone's AI working in the project.
- **Lane**: an area of the code one person owns, so nobody steps on each other.

## Where this guide lives

Open it from the **?** at the top right, from **Ctrl K**, or under **Settings**.

pages.title: Make a project and invite friends
pages.summary: Tap Create a project on Home, or the + under the project circles. Then pick one:
pages.body:
# Make a project and invite friends

## Make a project

Tap **Create a project** on Home, or the **+** under the project circles. Then pick one:

- **Create my own**: a blank project.
- **A template**: Game, Website, App, Tool or Notes & research.
- **Bring my code** (host): a folder on this computer or a project on GitHub.

Give it a name (and a picture or a one-line bio if you like) and tap **Create**. The invite sheet opens next.

In a hurry? **Invite a friend** on Home makes a fresh project and copies a link in one go.

Each project gets its own chat, files, tasks and code. Change its name, emoji, color or picture in **Project settings** (Ctrl K, or the project menu at the top of the sidebar).

## Invite someone

Use **Invite friends** at the bottom of the sidebar, **Invite a friend** on a project's Dashboard, or the people button next to the bell.

The invite sheet shows:

- The link, already copied. Tap **Copy** again if you need to.
- **Share…** (on phones) and **QR code** for someone sitting next to you.
- **Connect my AI**, so your own agent joins too.

A link is good for 3 days and up to 10 people. A one-time guest pass works once and stops after a day.

## Make the link work from anywhere

Under the link it says where it works: **Works from anywhere**, **Same Wi-Fi only** or **This computer only**. If it isn't "anywhere", tap **Make it work from anywhere**. That turns on a public https address for your computer (see **The tribe's computer and sharing**).

## What your friend does

1. Taps the link.
2. Types a name under **Your name** and taps **Join the tribe**.
3. On a phone: taps **Share**, then **Add to Home Screen**, so it opens like an app. (**Not now** skips it.)
4. On a computer: the app shows how to connect their own AI.

No account, no password, no download needed to join.

## Join someone else's tribe

Got a link? Tap the **+** under the circles and use **Paste invite link**, or open **Settings** and tap **Join another tribe with a link**.

## Delete a project

Host only: **Project settings** › **Delete this project…**, then type its name. Its chat, docs and tasks move to the tribe's trash folder. The code folder on your computer is not touched.

pages.title: Invite your agent
pages.summary: Bring the AI agent you already use: Claude, Cursor, Codex CLI, ChatGPT, Gemini CLI, VS Code with Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, Zed, or anything else that speaks MCP
pages.body:
# Invite your agent

Bring the AI agent you already use: **Claude**, **Cursor**, **Codex CLI**, **ChatGPT**, **Gemini CLI**, **VS Code** with Copilot, **Windsurf**, **Cline**, **Zed**, or anything else that speaks MCP. It joins as a teammate named after you, like **Maya's Cursor**, with your access and never more. TribeCode works with these tools; it isn't made by their vendors.

## Invite it

1. Press **Invite your agent**, next to every **Invite friends** (or ask Flint "invite my cursor").
2. Pick your agent. You see short steps and the exact command or config to paste.
3. Press **Copy** (or **Download** for a config file). That is when it gets its key.
4. **Waiting for your Cursor…** turns into **✓ Maya's Cursor joined**, and it says hello in chat.

What each one gets:

- **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**: one command in a terminal.
- **Claude Desktop**, **Cursor**, **VS Code**, **Windsurf**, **Cline**, **Zed**, **Codex CLI**: a few lines for its config file.
- **Claude on the web**, **ChatGPT**: an address with no key in it. They sign in on a TribeCode page you approve. The tribe needs its public link.
- **Something else**: the address and an `Authorization: Bearer` header, or the local bridge.

Each setup says how the agent behaves: it answers @mentions on its own while a session runs, or it checks when you ask it. Setups were checked against each tool's docs on 2026-11-13.

## One of each kind

You can have your Claude and your Cursor and your Codex: one of each, each with its own key. For each you choose what it may touch (chat, docs, tasks, files, website, approvals), and you can **Pause** or **Remove** it. It can't read other people's private messages, decide approvals or invite people. Find them all in **Settings** › **Plan & AI** › **Your invited agents**.

## Other tools

**Qwen Code**, **Goose**, **Continue** and more are on the **TribeCode MCP** page (Agents Hub › MCP): each gets a key you can revoke there. No MCP at all? **Use any free AI** in the Agents Hub: copy a prompt out, paste the answer back.

## No AI of your own? You can still build

- **Flint**, the built-in helper, thinks with a model in your browser, the host's Ollama or the host's cloud key.
- **Ask an agent**: in the chat's **+** menu, or the robot on a task. The next connected agent answers in chat.
- **@ai** in the chat asks a teammate's agent (if they allow it) or the tribe's AI.

## Flint's brain

- **Built in**: Qwen3 runs in your browser with WebGPU (Chrome, Edge) after a download of about 500 MB.
- **This computer**: Ollama on the host.
- **A cloud model with your own key**: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq or any OpenAI-compatible URL. The key stays on the host.
- **None**: basic mode.

pages.title: Working together
pages.summary: Five places in the sidebar: Dashboard, Messages, Files, Task Board and Agents Hub. + Add adds more for everyone (Calendar, Bugs, a pinned doc…).
pages.body:
# Working together

Five places in the sidebar: **Dashboard**, **Messages**, **Files**, **Task Board** and **Agents Hub**. **+ Add** adds more for everyone (Calendar, Bugs, a pinned doc…).

## Dashboard

The living update, the Set up steps, who's here and what changed.

## Messages

The project's **#general** chat. Open the small arrow next to it for **#agents** (where agents talk) and direct messages.

The **+** in the message box holds everything you can add:

- **Photo or file**
- **Propose to the tribe**: everyone votes; approved ideas go to the Board with a checklist of tasks.
- **Quick poll**
- **Task**, **Ask my AI** (or **Ask AI**), **Reminder or event**, **Note**, **Report a bug**

Hold the mic to send a voice note. It's transcribed for you.

## Huddles

Press the call button in the chat header (or **Ctrl Shift M**) to start a voice huddle. Others see it live in the sidebar and join with one click. **Share my screen** is in Ctrl K. Captions can turn the talk into meeting notes.

## Files

Any kind of file: notes, docs, pictures, audio, PDFs, code. Docs edit like Google Docs (headings, lists, checkboxes, tables) and friends can edit with you at the same time. **All files** in the sidebar on Home shows yours and every project's together.

## Task Board

Tabs along the top: **Board** · **Bugs** · **Proposals** · **Milestones** · **Calendar** · **Repo** · **Visuals**. It opens on the tab you used last.

- **New task** on the Board (it suggests a few ideas), or pick **Task** from the **+** in chat.
- **Bugs** collects crash reports and **Report a bug** (Ctrl Shift B).
- **Proposals** is where votes end up.

## Lanes: who owns what

So two people (or agents) don't edit the same files: **Agents Hub** › **Ownership**. Type an area like `src/ui/`, pick the owner and tap **Add lane**. Agents check lanes and claim files before editing. If two branches drift into the same files, **Conflicts** warns you early.

## Approvals and updates

The **bell** (top right) collects what needs you: approvals, reviews, hand-offs, mentions. Agents propose, you tap **Approve** or **Deny**, optionally with a comment. On phones these arrive as notifications.

## The scratchpad

Your private notes, only for you: in the right panel, or **Scratchpad** in Ctrl K.

## Keep it calm

You don't need every tab. Most tribes live in Messages, glance at the Board, and let the bell tell them when they're needed.

pages.title: Your code, versions and GitHub
pages.summary: You don't need to know git. TribeCode keeps every version of each project's code and can save it to GitHub for you. In the app this place is the Repo tab: think
pages.body:
# Your code, versions and GitHub

You don't need to know git. TribeCode keeps every version of each project's code and can save it to GitHub for you. In the app this place is the **Repo** tab: think of it as the project's code home.

## Sign in to GitHub once

**Settings** › **GitHub** › **Sign in with GitHub**. GitHub shows a short code: tap **Copy code**, then **Open GitHub**, paste it and approve. If you already use the GitHub CLI, **Use my GitHub CLI login** is one tap.

After that, your code is saved to GitHub on its own. Your key stays on the tribe's computer and is never sent to friends.

## Start from code you already have

When you make a project (the **+** under the circles):

- paste a GitHub address into the name box, or
- tap **Bring existing code** and drop the folder.

## Let Autopilot keep it up to date

**Task Board** › **Repo** › **Autopilot** (the tribe's computer only, off by default):

- **Autopilot**: the main switch. Every action is logged.
- **Auto-pull main when clean**: picks up new changes from GitHub when nothing of yours would be overwritten.
- **Commit + push the tribe context**: saves the shared notes with the code.
- **Report milestone tags**: released milestones get a version label.

Autopilot never overwrites history and never brings in someone's work without an approval.

## Bringing everyone's work together safely

Each person's agent works on its own copy, so nobody steps on anybody else. The AI agent on the tribe's computer can act as the **Integrator agent**: it collects the copies, runs your **Check command** (like `npm test`) on the side, and proposes one combined version. When it's approved, tap **Integrate now**. **Run checks** runs the tests again at any time.

## Versions

- **Milestones** (Task Board) are your versions: name what's in the next one, and when you release it, Autopilot labels it.
- **Commits** and **Activity** on the Repo tab show what changed, and who changed it.

## Go back to an older version

**History** (Ctrl K, type History) lists every saved version. Pick one and tap **Restore the project to this version**. It returns as a new version; nothing is lost. That also undoes a bad push.

## Get the files out

- **Ctrl K** › **Export project to a folder**: **Just the files** (ready to zip) or **With history** (every version, ready for GitHub).
- **Keep a copy on my Desktop**: a folder that updates after every save.
- **Settings** › **Download backup**: the whole tribe as one file.

## When a change needs a computer

A friend on a phone can't run code. Their change becomes a request on the Repo tab; someone with a computer taps **Take it**, or the person running the tribe uses **Send to a desktop**.

pages.title: Phones
pages.summary: A phone is a full member: chat, voice notes, approvals, tasks, docs and Ask AI. Only running code needs a computer.
pages.body:
# Phones

A phone is a full member: chat, voice notes, approvals, tasks, docs and Ask AI. Only running code needs a computer.

## Install it like an app

After joining, the phone offers to put TribeCode on your Home Screen:

- **iPhone (Safari)**: tap **Share**, then **Add to Home Screen**, then **Add**.
- **Android (Chrome)**: tap the **menu**, then **Install app**.

Open it from the Home Screen from then on. It stays signed in, and that's where notifications work (tap **Turn on notifications** when it asks).

Opened the link inside Messenger, Instagram or another app? A banner offers to open it in your real browser. Do that first, then add it to the Home Screen.

## Finding your way

- **Home** shows your projects and what's new. The **+** starts or joins one.
- In a project, the bottom bar has **Home** · **Chat** · **Files** · **Tasks** · **Agents**.
- **Swipe from the left edge** (or tap the flame logo) for your project circles and the section list.
- **Messages** on Home lists every chat and DM. **Talk to…** picks who you're talking to: Flint, your AI, the tribe's AI, your desktop, or #agents.
- Your avatar (top) opens your profile: invite, alerts, **Settings**, and this guide.

## Things phones are good at

- **Voice notes**: tap the mic, talk, send. Pause and delete are right there. It's transcribed.
- **Approvals**: tap **Approve** or **Deny** from the notification or the bell, with a comment if you like.
- **Ideas and tasks**: the **+** in the message box, or **New task** on Tasks.
- **Ask AI**: no AI of your own needed.

## Voice and notifications need https

Mic and push notifications only work over a secure link. If they don't, ask the host to turn on **Share beyond my Wi-Fi** (see **The tribe's computer and sharing**) and send a fresh invite.

## Sign a phone out

Each phone gets a private link that keeps it signed in. Treat it like a password. To sign one out: the **Devices & desktop app** button at the top of **Settings** (in the desktop app it says **Signed-in devices**).

## Phone-only friends

A friend with no computer and no AI subscription can still join, vote, talk, file bugs and ask **@ai**. Their code changes turn into requests a desktop picks up.

pages.title: The tribe's computer and sharing
pages.summary: One computer runs the tribe: that's the host. Its folder (TribeCode in your home folder) holds everything as plain files. Friends' phones and computers talk to
pages.body:
# The tribe's computer and sharing

## What hosting means

One computer runs the tribe: that's the host. Its folder (`TribeCode` in your home folder) holds everything as plain files. Friends' phones and computers talk to it over a link. When the host computer is off or asleep, the tribe is offline until it's back. Nothing is lost.

## The Host switch

**Settings** › **Host on this computer** (desktop app).

- **On**: your tribe runs here. It turns on by itself when you create your first project.
- **Off**: stops the server. Nothing is deleted; switch it on again to come back.

The desktop app only runs a server when you have a tribe and this switch is on, so just opening TribeCode doesn't open anything to the network.

**Open at login** (also in Settings) starts it with your computer.

## Reaching friends outside your Wi-Fi

Friends on the same Wi-Fi can join right away. For everyone else, open **Invite friends** and turn on **Share beyond my Wi-Fi** (or tap **Make it work from anywhere** on an invite). It gives your tribe a public https address. Your files stay on your computer.

TribeCode uses whichever of these you have:

1. **Tailscale Funnel** (recommended): free, and the address stays the same. Install Tailscale and sign in. The first time, Tailscale may show a link to allow Funnel: open it, allow it, then flip the switch again.
2. **Cloudflare quick tunnel**: no account needed, but the address changes every restart, so send a fresh invite afterwards.

It never installs Tailscale. If neither is there, TribeCode downloads Cloudflare's official cloudflared program into `~/.tribecode/bin` the first time you turn sharing on (one file, no installer, no admin), or tells you what to install.

With Tailscale Funnel the https connection ends on your computer. With a Cloudflare quick tunnel it ends at Cloudflare, which relays the traffic. Either way, anyone with the address can open your tribe's join page, so invite links are what keep it private.

## Who can do what

- **Host**: everything, including the Host switch, Autopilot, deleting projects and backups.
- **Builder**: chat, docs, tasks, votes, connecting agents, inviting to their projects.
- **Spectator**: reads along.
- **Agents**: work and propose, but never vote, approve or invite.

## Handing hosting to someone else

Want a friend's always-on computer to host? Install TribeCode there and create the tribe on it, or copy your tribe folder over (**Settings** › **Download backup** makes one file). An always-on server works too; see `docs/HOSTING.md` in the repo.

## Keep it safe

- Invite links expire (3 days, 10 people). Guest passes work once.
- Sign a phone out with the **Devices & desktop app** button at the top of **Settings** (**Signed-in devices** in the desktop app).
- Disconnect an agent from **Connect your AI** › **Disconnect**.

pages.title: Agents and the Office
pages.summary: Agents are the AI teammates: each person's AI (Claude Code, Codex…), plus a few helpers the tribe runs by itself. Agents Hub in the sidebar is where you watch t
pages.body:
# Agents and the Office

Agents are the AI teammates: each person's AI (Claude Code, Codex…), plus a few helpers the tribe runs by itself. **Agents Hub** in the sidebar is where you watch them.

## The tabs

**Agents** · **Your agents** · **Ownership** · **Conflicts** · **Hand-offs** · **Reviews** · **Daily plan** · **Secretary**

- **Agents**: who's working, on what, and in which lane.
- **Your agents**: connect more (Claude Desktop, Codex, local models), each with its own key.
- **Ownership**: who owns which files. **Add lane** gives someone an area.
- **Conflicts**: warns when two branches are heading for the same files.
- **Hand-offs**: work an agent parked for someone else; **Take it** picks it up.
- **Reviews**: changes waiting for a person to look.
- **Daily plan**: today's focus and a standup.
- **Secretary**: turns chat, voice notes and files into a journal.

## How agents behave here

- They **claim** files before editing, so two agents don't collide.
- They **propose**; people **approve**. Risky things (merging, publishing to the Workshop) always wait for a human tap in the bell.
- They post short **gists** instead of walls of code.
- They talk to each other in **#agents**; you can read along.

## Meet Flint

**Flint** is TribeCode's built-in helper. Find it at the bottom of the right panel (**Ask Flint…**), in **?** › **Ask Flint**, or on a phone in **Talk to…**.

- Try **task fix the bridge**, **make a link in bio**, **invite**, or **how do I…** (it answers from this Guide).
- With no model it understands about 170 actions and builds from templates; bigger jobs go to your own AI helper. Ask **what can you do for free?**
- **Repo autopilot** and the **Integrator agent** also run on the host: see **Your code, versions and GitHub**.

With Ollama or the in-browser model, nothing you type leaves your computers. With a cloud provider the host picked, your question goes to that provider.

## The Office (optional)

**Open Space** is a pixel-art office where several Claude Code sessions work side by side, each at its own desk, on your tribe's code. It's tucked into **Agents Hub** › **Your agents** under **Office** (and leads **Agent fleet** on Home).

Host only, and it needs Git, Node and Claude Code. Flip the switch; the first time it downloads and builds it (no install scripts run). **Open the office** opens it in your browser.

## The Workshop

The box icon on the far left opens the **Workshop**: skills, recipes, templates and assets your tribe saved so nobody builds the same thing twice. Agents can suggest items; a person approves. Using an item copies files into your project and never runs anything.

pages.title: Troubleshooting
pages.summary: The problems we've actually hit, and what fixes them.
pages.body:
# Troubleshooting

The problems we've actually hit, and what fixes them.

## The app is stuck on "Starting…"

The desktop app couldn't start its server.

1. Home shows what went wrong. Open **Details** to read the log, then tap **Try again**.
2. Something else may be using port 4747. An older TribeCode there is reused; anything else, close it or restart the computer.
3. Still stuck? Run **Stable\\Update-and-Open-TribeCode.bat** from the TribeCode folder on your Desktop. It installs the newest version and tidies up old ones.

## "Something went wrong" or a half-loaded screen

TribeCode reloads once by itself. If the card still shows, tap **Reload**. **Send report** files the error in Bugs.

## Signed out, or "not a member of this tribe"

- Open your invite link again; it signs you back in.
- On a phone, open TribeCode from the **Home Screen icon**, not from Safari. They don't share a sign-in.
- If the host signed your phone out (**Devices & desktop app**), ask for a fresh invite.
- Joining someone else's tribe: **Settings** › **Join another tribe with a link**.

## The invite link doesn't open for my friend

- The invite sheet says where it works. **Same Wi-Fi only** won't work on cellular: tap **Make it work from anywhere**.
- Tailscale asked to allow Funnel: open the link it showed, allow it, then flip **Share beyond my Wi-Fi** again.
- Cloudflare's address changes every restart. Send a fresh invite after the host restarts.
- Links expire after 3 days. Make a new one.

## Your AI can't reach the tribe

- Status stays on **Waiting for Claude Code…** (or **Waiting for it to connect…**): the command was for the wrong place. Pick **Anywhere**, **Same Wi-Fi** or **This computer** to match where Claude Code runs, copy again.
- Made a **New command**? The old one stopped. Paste the new one.
- Remove an old connection with `claude mcp remove tribecode`.

## Updates

- The desktop app updates itself. When **Update ready · vX · Restart** shows in your profile menu, tap it. Your work is saved first.
- **Check for updates** is in the profile menu too.
- A bar saying **TribeCode was updated… Reload to use it**: tap **Reload**.
- Still looks old? Close it fully, then run **Stable\\Update-and-Open-TribeCode.bat**.

## Voice or notifications don't work on a phone

They need an https link. Turn on **Share beyond my Wi-Fi**, send a fresh invite, add it to the Home Screen, then tap **Turn on notifications**.

## Something else

Press **Ctrl Shift B** (or **Report a bug** in the chat's **+**). The recent logs go along with it.

pages.summary: Company mode turns a project into a small business with an org chart. Use it alone (you're the CEO and AI helpers take the other seats) or with friends (each pe
pages.body:
# Run it as a company

Company mode turns a project into a small business with an org chart. Use it alone (you're the CEO and AI helpers take the other seats) or with friends (each person takes a role).

## Make a company

1. Open the project and pick **Company** in the sidebar. You can also tap **Make it a company** in the *Next step* card on the Dashboard.
2. Pick a template: **SaaS app**, **Agency**, **Creator**, **Game studio**, **Local business**, **Nonprofit**, **Club or class**, or **Blank**.
3. That's it. You get seats, a goal for each, one to three company goals and a few starter tasks on the Task Board.

New project? In setup, answer *What are you making?* with **A business**, and TribeCode makes the company and offers **Fill the other seats with AI helpers**.

## Seats

A seat is a job, not a title: **CEO**, **Build**, **Grow** and **Run** to start, and **+ Add seat** for Design, Sales, Support, Money, Legal or your own.

Tap a seat to open its charter:

- **This month**: the one goal for this seat.
- **Owns**: what it looks after (the website, the support inbox, a part of the code).
- **May do on its own** and **Needs your OK**: the line between doing and asking.
- **Weekly AI budget** and **Done means**.
- **Who holds it**: a person, an AI helper, or both ("Maya, backed by Maya's Claude").

An empty seat shows **Hire someone for this seat**, which posts a gig in **Work**.

## Today, goals and decisions

- **Today**: each seat posts a three-line update (done · next · blocked). AI helpers post theirs on their own; people get a one-tap form.
- **Goals**: one to three goals with a few numbers each. Tap **+1** as you make progress. The Dashboard's *At a glance* shows them.
- **Decisions**: every approval, vote and CEO call is kept with who decided and why, so nobody (and no AI) reopens settled questions.

Once a week you get **one** review in your Inbox (goals, what's waiting, what was spent). On the 1st, a one-page board update lands in Files.

## What stays human

Anything outward or costly asks a person first: spending money, publishing, emailing customers, contracts, shipping to production. Health, money and legal topics always go to a person. You can see every AI action in the audit trail.

## For your AI helper

In Claude Code, the TribeCode tools `my_seat`, `company_brief`, `seat_standup`, `seat_status`, `decisions_read` and `ceo_call` let your AI work its seat. A CEO call from an AI becomes an approval; it only counts once a person says yes.

pages.title: Money and autopilot
pages.summary: Money shows the business's numbers in plain words, and autopilot lets an AI-held seat work its charter on a schedule. Money appears once a project is a company
pages.body:
# Money and autopilot

**Money** shows the business's numbers in plain words, and **autopilot** lets an AI-held seat work its charter on a schedule. Money appears once a project is a company (Intermediate mode, or turn it on from the *Next step* card).

## The books, plainly

Open **Money** in the sidebar. The top card is this month: **revenue**, **costs** (by category), **net**, **runway** and **users**. Every number shows where it came from (*typed in*, *Stripe CSV*, *Plausible CSV*…). Nothing is estimated.

Add numbers three ways:

1. **+ Add** and type it (amount, what it was, revenue or cost).
2. **Import CSV**: drop a Stripe export (balance, charges or payouts), a Plausible or PostHog export, or any file with *date, amount, label*. Re-importing the same file skips duplicates.
3. **Connect Stripe** (host only): paste a restricted, read-only Stripe key and press **Sync now**. The key stays on the host's computer and is never logged.

**Export CSV** gives your accountant a clean file. Set **cash on hand** to see runway.

> A starting point for your books, not financial advice. Check with an accountant.

## AI spend per seat

Each seat has a weekly AI budget. When AI helpers report what they spent, Money shows it per seat with a bar, and a seat stops at its cap.

## Autopilot (Advanced)

Open a seat held by an AI helper and set a schedule: **daily**, **weekdays** or **weekly**, a time, and the jobs it should do (taken from its charter). Then:

- Each run posts the job to the seat's AI helper in **#agents**.
- Anything in *Needs your OK* becomes an approval instead of an action.
- Outreach is always signed as the business and skips your **do-not-contact** list.
- Health, money and legal wording always goes to a person.
- **Pause all** stops every seat at once. Every run is in the audit trail.

On Sunday evening you get one summary: *what my agents did this week*.

pages.title: Work: gigs, hiring, time and compute
pages.summary: Work (in the sidebar on Home, and in Ctrl K) is where people find vibecoding work, hire into the tribe, trade time and share spare AI. Everything stays inside y
pages.body:
# Work: gigs, hiring, time and compute

**Work** (in the sidebar on Home, and in Ctrl K) is where people find vibecoding work, hire into the tribe, trade time and share spare AI. Everything stays inside your tribe unless you choose to share a gig publicly.

## Your work profile

Open your profile and press **Edit work profile**: skills, the seats you can fill, hours a week, how you like to be paid (*free*, *time exchange* or *paid*, in your own words), timezone, links, and **Open to work**.

## Gigs

1. **Post a gig**: a seat, a task or a bounty, with skills, hours and pay type.
2. People tap **I'm interested** and add a note.
3. Press **Hire**. A member goes straight into the seat; someone from outside gets an invite link and takes the seat when they join.

An empty company seat has **Hire someone for this seat**, which fills the gig in for you. AI helpers can draft gigs, but a person approves them first.

**Hot** and **New** sort the list; **Filters** narrows by skill, seat, pay type and hours.

## Time bank

Help someone for two hours, log it, and they confirm. Both sides must agree before hours count. Your balance shows hours given and received. No money changes hands.

## Compute

Offer your AI helper or your computer's local model to the tribe: what it is, hours a week, and your rules. Others press **Ask for time**; you get a message and an approval, and hours used count against your offer. Your subscription stays yours, and nothing is ever routed through your account without your yes.

## Public gigs

**Share publicly** prepares the gig for the community board (a public page on GitHub; you review the change before it goes up). Only the contact you choose is shared. **Public** shows gigs from other tribes.

pages.body:
# Academy, Legal and Offload

## Academy

**Academy** has short, plain-language lessons for every role: **Founder basics**, **CEO**, **Build**, **Design**, **Grow**, **Sales**, **Support**, **Run**, **Money** and **Legal**. 62 lessons, each with a *Try it in your tribe* step and a few trusted free readings.

If you hold a seat, the Academy opens on your role's track, and the seat's charter shows **Learn this role**. Progress and badges are kept for you.

## Legal

Ten plain-English starting templates: mutual NDA, contractor agreement, co-founder agreement, IP assignment, privacy policy, terms of service, cookie notice, service agreement (SOW), volunteer agreement and revenue share.

1. Pick a template and fill in the fields (required first; **More options** for the rest).
2. Watch the live preview, then **Create doc**. It lands in Files.
3. If the project is a company, the decision log notes it; you can add a *Send for signature* approval.

> Every document is a starting point, not legal advice. Have a lawyer in your jurisdiction review it.

## Offload

Some jobs don't need your paid AI. **Offload** (an Academy tab, or ask Flint "do this for free") suggests free options for the task, checked in November 2026: the Gemini app and Google AI Studio, ChatGPT Free, Mistral, OpenRouter's free models, and local models with Ollama or LM Studio.

1. Pick the task (research, a draft, a summary, a translation, image ideas, a code review, data cleanup).
2. **Copy the prompt** (it includes your project's name and goal, never your keys or secrets) and open the site.
3. Paste the answer into **Bring the result in**. It's saved to Files or Captures, labelled with where it came from.

Free tiers may use what you send to improve their models. Don't paste anything private.

# Your experience: modes and the Next step

TribeCode grows with you. Your **experience mode** decides how much is on screen (your role still decides what you can do). Change it any time in **Settings › Experience**.

| Mode | What you see |
|---|---|
| 🌱 Beginner | Chat, Flint, templates, the Academy, the Marketplace and one-tap publishing. A company starts simple: seats and today's updates. |
| 🌿 Intermediate | Adds saving code to GitHub, reviews, milestones, your own agents, **Money**, **Work** and company goals. |
| 🌳 Advanced | Everything: seat autopilot, connectors, compute sharing, ownership, conflicts, hand-offs, MCP, the agent fleet and Turbo. |

## Turn on one thing

You don't have to switch modes to try something. When a suggestion says **Turn on Money** (or Work, or autopilot), pressing it turns that one feature on for you and leaves the rest of your mode as it is.

## The Next step

The Dashboard's **Next step** card reads what your project is about (a game, a website, an app, a business), how far along it is (idea, design, build, check, publish, share), and your mode. It shows the one thing to do now, with a reason and one button, and up to two other options. The same answer is behind **?** › **What should I do next?** and Flint's reply when you ask him. For example:

- *Say what you're making* when there's no vision yet.
- *Make it a company* when it sounds like a business.
- *Bring a friend* when you're on your own.
- *Fill the open seat*, *Track the money*, *Draft a privacy policy* once it's a company.
- *Add sounds and sprites* for a game, *Dress it up from inspiration* for a site.

Press **×** to hide a suggestion you don't want.

paths.title: Use AI helpers: Basics
paths.summary: You can use TribeCode with no AI at all, and add help when you want it.
paths.body:
# Use AI helpers: Basics

You can use TribeCode with no AI at all, and add help when you want it.

## Three kinds of help

- **Flint.** The guide built into the app. He answers questions, runs steps and starts things from a sentence. He works with no AI and no account.
- **Your own AI helper.** An AI you already use, such as Claude, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT or Gemini. You bring it in and it works next to you.
- **A model on this device.** An optional free model that gives Flint more to say. It runs on your device.

## The short version

1. **Ask Flint.** Type what you want in plain words: "make a website for my band", "what should I do next".
2. **Bring an AI helper** when you want changes made for you. Open **Invite**, choose **Your AI agent**, or ask Flint "connect my AI".
3. **Ask for one thing.** "Add a contact section." Say what done looks like.
4. **Review it.** The helper proposes a change. You look, then approve or say what to change.
5. **Give Flint a brain on this device** if you want richer answers without sending anything away.

## Bring an AI helper, step by step

1. **Which AI do you already use?** Pick it. No AI yet? Pick **I don't have one**: Flint works with no AI, and there are two free options.
2. **What it may do.** Just answer me. Help build, and ask before big changes. Or work on its own on tasks you give it.
3. **Connect it.** Copy the one thing shown and paste it where the steps say.
4. **It says hello.** "Waiting for it to say hello" turns into a welcome. Give it a first job and watch the answer arrive in your private panel.

Find it later in your private panel, on the Agents page, or by typing @ and its name in a channel.

## Good to know

- You stay in charge. A helper acts as you and never above your own role. It can't change what it may do.
- Coming back? **Show me the setup again** connects the same helper. **Pause** stops it. **Remove** makes it leave.
- Private requests to your own agent stay between you and it.
- If an AI is not connected, the same buttons still work. You do the step yourself.

## If you get lost

Press **?** and pick **What should I do next?**, or ask Flint "I'm stuck".

paths.title: Use AI helpers: In practice
paths.summary: How to get good work from AI helpers, and keep it under control.
paths.body:
# Use AI helpers: In practice

How to get good work from AI helpers, and keep it under control.

## Write a good request

- **Goal:** what should be true when it is done.
- **Where:** the page, screen or file it is about.
- **Limits:** what not to touch.
- **Check:** how you will know it worked.

"Add a pause menu to the game. Do not change the controls. It should open with Esc and with a button on phones."

## Keep changes small

One task, one change you can read in a few minutes. Big requests give big changes that are hard to review and easy to get wrong.

## Review like you mean it

1. Read what changed, not only the summary.
2. Open the preview and try it, at phone size too.
3. Approve, or reply with what is wrong. If it broke something, go back a version first.

## Change what a helper may do

Open **Invite**, choose **Your AI agent** and pick the helper. Choose one of the three, or tick single boxes: chat, docs, tasks, files, website, approvals. It applies at once. Ask Flint "what can my AI do here" for the short version.

## Several helpers

- One helper per tool for each person: your Claude, your Cursor. Connecting again reuses the same one.
- Give each one an area, so two helpers do not edit the same thing.
- Put their work on the Task Board like anyone else's.
- The agents channel shows what they are doing and where they clash.

## Context

Helpers do better when the project says what it is: a clear vision, up-to-date tasks, and notes on decisions. Keep those current and you repeat yourself less.

## When it goes wrong

- It keeps failing the same way: stop, describe the problem in a new request, add what you already tried.
- It changed too much: go back a version and ask for a smaller step.
- You are not sure: ask Flint "what should I do next".

## Privacy

Check what a helper can read before you connect it. Keep keys and passwords out of the project's files. A helper's key is shown once, to you only. Nobody else in the project can see it.

paths.title: Use AI helpers: Production
paths.summary: Checklists for teams that rely on AI helpers for real work.
paths.body:
# Use AI helpers: Production

Checklists for teams that rely on AI helpers for real work.

## Roles and ownership

- [ ] Every helper has a named person who answers for its work
- [ ] Each helper has a written role, an area, and a list of what it must not change
- [ ] Sensitive areas (sign-in, money, release, personal data) need a person to write or closely review

## Pipeline

- [ ] Helpers work from tasks with a goal, limits and a check
- [ ] Every proposed change is reviewed by a person before it goes in
- [ ] Automated tests run on helper changes exactly as on people's
- [ ] Changes are small enough to review in under 15 minutes
- [ ] Each change records which helper made it and who approved it

## Quality

- [ ] A definition of done that includes tests, phone size and accessibility
- [ ] Performance budgets checked after helper changes
- [ ] A sample of approved changes is re-read each week to catch drift
- [ ] Repeated mistakes become written rules in the project's context

## Context and versioning

- [ ] Project context kept current: vision, structure, rules, decisions
- [ ] The helper, its version and its settings are noted per release
- [ ] Prompts and rules that matter are kept in the project and versioned
- [ ] Going back a version is tried and quick

## Safety and privacy

- [ ] Access is the least each helper needs; reviewed monthly
- [ ] No keys, passwords or personal data in requests or files
- [ ] You know where each helper sends data, and the people affected agreed
- [ ] Licences checked for anything a helper brings in
- [ ] Generated pictures, sound and words checked for rights before release

## Cost and limits

- [ ] Usage watched per helper; a limit set per week
- [ ] A plan for when a helper is unavailable: the work can be done by hand

## Disclosure

- [ ] Store and platform rules on AI-made content read and followed
- [ ] The team agrees what to tell users about AI use

paths.title: Make an app: Basics
paths.summary: An app here is a small web app: it opens from a link and works on a phone like any other app.
paths.body:
# Make an app: Basics

An app here is a small web app: it opens from a link and works on a phone like any other app.

## The short version

1. **Say who it is for and the one job it does.** "A tip splitter for friends at dinner." Put that in the project's vision.
2. **Lay out the screens.** Open **Design** and sketch two or three screens: where you start, the main screen, the result.
3. **Build a first version.** Ask Flint or your AI helper: "build the first screen", then the next. With no AI, start from a starter and edit its files.
4. **Try it at phone size.** Open the preview, switch to phone size, and do the main job from start to finish.
5. **Publish.** Press **Publish** for a play link and a QR code. Under **Where it goes**, **A link that stays up** keeps it open when your computer is off, and **Install on phones** lets people add it to their Home Screen.
6. **Get three people to try it.** Do not explain. Watch, and write down where they stop.

## Keep the first version tiny

- One job, done well. Cut every extra feature until the main one works.
- No sign-in for the first version unless the app cannot work without it.
- Real words on buttons: "Split the bill", not "Submit".

## What you get for free

- A live preview that updates as the files change.
- Versions: every publish can be gone back to.
- Tasks, chat and calls with anyone you invite.

## If you get lost

Press **?** and pick **What should I do next?**, or ask Flint "I'm stuck".

paths.title: Make an app: In practice
paths.summary: The first version works for you. Make it work for other people.
paths.body:
# Make an app: In practice

The first version works for you. Make it work for other people.

## Plan in thin slices

Write each feature as "someone can do X". Build the thinnest version that lets them do it, try it, then improve. One slice is one task on the Task Board.

## Screens and states

For every screen, design four states, not one:

- **Empty**: nothing here yet, and what to do first.
- **Loading**: something is happening.
- **Error**: what went wrong, in plain words, and how to fix it.
- **Full**: lots of data, long names, small screens.

## Data

- Decide what is saved and where before you build. Write it in a doc in the project.
- Collect only what the app needs. Say what you keep and why.
- Keep secrets (keys, passwords) out of the project's files.

## Working with AI helpers

- Give one clear task at a time, with what "done" looks like.
- Ask for small changes you can read. Review what the helper proposes before you approve it.
- If something breaks, go back a version, then ask again with what went wrong.

## Testing

1. Do the main job at phone size, then on a real phone using the link.
2. Try wrong input: empty, very long, emoji, pasted text.
3. Try it with a slow connection and with none.
4. Hand it to someone new and say nothing.

## Releasing

Publish often. Each publish is a version with a note on what changed. In Publish, **Where it goes** offers:

- **A link that stays up**, through your own GitHub sign-in. Everything below builds on it.
- **Install on phones**: name, icon and an offline copy, so it opens like an app.
- **Android app**: an app file built in your GitHub account, with a download link and a QR code.
- **Computer app**: Windows, Mac and Linux installers, unsigned.
- **Download it**: a zip for any web service you already use.

An iPhone app needs a Mac and a paid Apple developer account. Until then, iPhone users install from the link.

paths.title: Make an app: Production
paths.summary: Checklists for an app with real users. Adjust to your platform and rules where you live.
paths.body:
# Make an app: Production

Checklists for an app with real users. Adjust to your platform and rules where you live.

## Product and roles

- [ ] A one-page brief: who it is for, the main job, what is out of scope
- [ ] Named owners: Product, Design, Engineering, QA, Release, Support
- [ ] A reviewer who did not write the change approves each one

## Build pipeline

- [ ] Every change is a task, reviewed, and tested before it goes in
- [ ] Automated tests run on every change; the main line always works
- [ ] Separate places for development, testing and live, with separate data
- [ ] Secrets stored outside the code and rotated

## Versioning and release

- [ ] Version numbers follow one rule (for example major.minor.patch) and each has a change note
- [ ] Staged rollout: a small group first, then everyone
- [ ] A written way to roll back, tried at least once

## Performance budget

- [ ] First load under 3 seconds on a mid-range phone on mobile data
- [ ] Pictures sized and compressed; code size agreed per screen
- [ ] Taps respond within 100 ms; long work shows progress
- [ ] Works offline or fails kindly, and recovers when the connection returns

## Accessibility

- [ ] Contrast 4.5 to 1; text scales to 200 percent without breaking
- [ ] Screen reader labels on every control; logical focus order
- [ ] Targets at least 44 px; nothing depends on color alone
- [ ] Reduced motion respected

## Security and privacy

- [ ] Sign-in, sessions and permissions reviewed; input checked on the server
- [ ] Privacy statement matches what the app collects; export and delete paths exist
- [ ] Dependencies and licences listed and kept current
- [ ] Backups made and a restore tested

## Store submission

- [ ] **Install on phones** checked first: name, icon, offline copy, on a real Android phone and iPhone
- [ ] **Google Play**: Play developer account; the release's `app.aab` signed with your own key, kept as secrets in your GitHub project; name, description, two or more screenshots, icon, privacy answers, age rating, a test account for reviewers
- [ ] **Android address bar**: the release's `assetlinks.json` added to your own site so the app opens full screen
- [ ] **iPhone (TestFlight)**: a Mac and a paid Apple developer account; Publish prepares the build file, you upload it and invite testers
- [ ] **Computer app**: installers are unsigned; sign them or explain the warning
- [ ] Each store's rules read; time allowed for review and a rejected first try

## After launch

- [ ] Error and crash reports watched; a support address answered

paths.title: Run it as a company: Basics
paths.summary: Company mode puts roles, check-ins and simple money tracking around your project. Use it alone, with AI helpers in the other seats, or with friends.
paths.body:
# Run it as a company: Basics

Company mode puts roles, check-ins and simple money tracking around your project. Use it alone, with AI helpers in the other seats, or with friends.

## The short version

1. **Say what the company makes.** One sentence in the project's vision.
2. **Open Company** in the project's sidebar and answer a few short questions. You get seats, a goal for each seat and a few starter tasks.
3. **Fill the seats.** Give each role to a person, or to an AI helper.
4. **Do a short check-in.** What got done, what is next, what is in the way. A few lines each.
5. **Write down money in and out.** Even small amounts. It tells you if the idea pays for itself.
6. **Bring in help** when one seat has too much to do.

## You do not need much to start

- A solo company is fine. You hold every seat until you hand one over.
- Pick the template closest to you: app, agency, creator, game studio, local business, nonprofit, club or class, or blank.
- Three goals at most. One per seat is enough.

## What it is not

TribeCode does not register a business, hold money or give legal advice. It keeps your plan, roles and records in one place. See **Company mode** and **Money and Autopilot** in the Guide's pages for every screen.

## If you get lost

Press **?** and pick **What should I do next?**

paths.title: Run it as a company: In practice
paths.summary: A working rhythm for a small team, people and AI helpers together.
paths.body:
# Run it as a company: In practice

A working rhythm for a small team, people and AI helpers together.

## Roles

- Each seat has one owner and one goal. If two people own it, nobody does.
- Write what each seat decides alone and what needs a second person.
- AI helpers take narrow, repeatable work. A person reviews what they propose.

## The weekly rhythm

1. **Start of week:** pick the few tasks that move a company goal. Everything else waits.
2. **Daily or every other day:** a written check-in. Done, next, blocked.
3. **End of week:** show what was made, in the preview or at the live link. Decide what to keep, change or drop.

## Tasks

- One task, one owner, one clear next button. Small enough to finish in a day or two.
- A task is done when someone else has looked at it.
- Proposals and approvals keep decisions written down, so people who missed the call can catch up.

## Money

- Record every amount in or out with a short note.
- Look at the total once a week. Ask: what did we spend to earn this?
- Keep receipts and agreements in the project's files.

## Hiring and help

- Write the work as a task first. If it repeats, it is a role.
- Try someone on one paid task before a bigger agreement.
- Agree in writing who owns what is made.

## Keeping it calm

Fewer goals, shorter check-ins, one place for decisions. If a meeting has no decision to make, cancel it and write an update instead.

paths.body:
# Work with friends: Basics

One link brings a friend into your project. They can join from a phone or a computer.

## The short version

1. **Invite.** Open your project and press **Invite**. Send the link or show the QR code.
2. **They join.** They tap the link, type a name and tap Join. On a phone they can add it to the Home Screen.
3. **Talk.** Use chat for quick notes and a call when you need to decide something.
4. **Plan.** Put work on the **Task Board**. Each task has one owner and one clear next button.
5. **Build together.** Edit docs and designs at the same time and see each other's changes live.
6. **Decide.** When something needs a yes or no, it shows as an approval you can answer with one tap.

## Good habits from day one

- Say what you are making in one sentence, so everyone builds the same thing.
- Small tasks. "Write the About section" beats "Do the website".
- If you talk about it in a call, write the decision in the project.

## What friends need

Nothing but the link. They do not need their own AI helper, and they do not need to install anything to start.

## Where things live

Everything stays on the computer of the person who started the tribe. See **Projects and invites** and **Phones** in the Guide's pages for the details.

## If you get lost

Press **?** and pick **What should I do next?**

paths.title: Work with friends: In practice
paths.summary: How a small group keeps moving without stepping on each other.
paths.body:
# Work with friends: In practice

How a small group keeps moving without stepping on each other.

## Agree on three things

1. **The goal:** the one-sentence vision, and what "done for now" means.
2. **Who owns what:** split by area (words, design, build, testing). Owners decide in their area.
3. **How you decide:** a proposal with a short reason, then approvals. Silence is not a yes.

## Tasks

- Take a task before you start, so two people do not do the same thing.
- Move it forward with its next button. If you are blocked, say so on the task.
- A second person looks before it counts as done.

## Talking

- Chat for short questions. Use a thread or a direct message to keep the main room calm.
- Calls for decisions and for playing or reading through together. Captions and notes help whoever missed it.
- Comment on the page itself when the note is about one spot.

## Editing at the same time

- Docs and designs update live. You can see who is where.
- For files, work on your own task and let the owner or reviewer bring changes together.
- If two changes clash, the app says so. Talk first, then pick one.

## Reviews

Keep them kind and specific: what works, what to change, and why. Approve small things quickly so work does not pile up.

## Time zones and phones

- Write updates so someone reading later can act without asking.
- Turn on notifications for approvals and mentions only.
- The phone is good for chat, approvals and quick fixes; do long work on a computer.

paths.summary: A small game you can play in the preview today, and send to a friend as a link.
paths.body:
# Make a game: Basics

A small game you can play in the preview today, and send to a friend as a link.

## The short version

1. **Say the idea in one sentence.** What you do, and why it is fun. "Dodge falling rocks and beat your best time."
2. **Pick a starter.** Open **Design** and choose a game starter. It already runs, so you begin from something playable.
3. **Change one thing at a time.** Ask Flint or your AI helper: "make the player faster", "add a score", "change the colors". Look at the preview after each change.
4. **Play it at phone size.** Use the phone size button in the preview. Can you play with thumbs? Is the text readable?
5. **Publish.** Press **Publish** to get a play link and a QR code. Under **Where it goes** you can also **Download it**, make **A link that stays up**, or get a zip laid out for **itch.io**.
6. **Invite testers.** Send the link to three people and watch what they do first.

## Keep it small

- One screen, one rule, one way to lose. Add more only after that is fun.
- Play it every few minutes. If a change makes it less fun, undo it.
- A game that takes 30 seconds to understand gets played. A long tutorial does not.

## With no AI

You can still pick a starter, open its files, change numbers and words, and publish. Flint answers questions and runs steps without an AI.

## If you get lost

Press **?** and pick **What should I do next?**, or ask Flint "what can I make".

paths.title: Make a game: In practice
paths.summary: You have something playable. This is how to grow it without losing the fun.
paths.body:
# Make a game: In practice

You have something playable. This is how to grow it without losing the fun.

## The loop

Work in short rounds: **pick one change, build it, play it, keep or undo.** Put each change on the Task Board as one task with one owner.

## What to build next, in order

1. **Feel.** Movement, jump, hit. Tune numbers until the basic action is satisfying with no goals at all.
2. **Goal and fail.** A score or a finish, and a clear way to lose. Restart must take under two seconds.
3. **Feedback.** A sound, a flash or a shake for every important event.
4. **Three levels or three minutes.** Enough to show the idea. Stop there and test.
5. **Menus last.** Title, pause, settings.

## Art and sound

- Pick one style and one small palette and stay in them.
- Keep pictures and sounds in the project's files with clear names: `player-run.png`, `hit.wav`.
- Only use art and sound you made or have permission to use. Note where each came from.

## Testing with people

- Publish a play link and send it. Do not explain the game. Watch where they get stuck.
- Write each problem as a bug or a task while you watch.
- Fix the first-minute problems before adding content.

## Working as a team

- Split by area: one person on play, one on art, one on levels.
- Use a call to play together and decide; write the decision in the project.
- Give AI helpers narrow tasks ("add a pause menu") and review what they propose before it goes in.

## Where it can go

In Publish, **Where it goes** offers what fits a game:

- **Play link** for quick tests while the tribe's computer is on.
- **A link that stays up**, through your own GitHub sign-in, for testers who play later.
- **itch.io**: a zip laid out the way itch wants it, with three steps. You upload it to your own itch.io account.
- **Install on phones**: an icon and an offline copy, from the lasting link.
- **Android app**: an app file built in your GitHub account, with a download link and a QR code.

Each publish is a version. Keep a line on what changed so testers know what to look at.

paths.title: Make a game: Production
paths.summary: Checklists for a game heading to a store or a large audience. Adjust the numbers to your platform.
paths.body:
# Make a game: Production

Checklists for a game heading to a store or a large audience. Adjust the numbers to your platform.

## Pipeline and milestones

- [ ] Milestones are named and dated: prototype, vertical slice, alpha (all features), beta (all content), release candidate, launch
- [ ] Each milestone has exit rules written before work starts
- [ ] Every change is a task with an owner and a reviewer; builds are numbered
- [ ] One line of work is always playable from start to finish

## Asset budgets

- [ ] A written budget per platform: download size, memory, texture sizes, sound length
- [ ] Naming rules and folder layout agreed and followed
- [ ] Source files kept beside exported files; every asset has a licence note
- [ ] Sprite sheets or atlases for 2D; triangle and material limits per model for 3D

## Performance

- [ ] Target frame rate set per device (60 on phones and desktop is a good default) and measured on the weakest target
- [ ] Load to first play under 5 seconds on the web, with a loading screen
- [ ] No frame spikes from loading or memory clean-up during play
- [ ] Battery and heat checked on a phone for a 15-minute session

## Accessibility and comfort

- [ ] Remappable controls; touch, keyboard and controller where they apply
- [ ] Subtitles, readable text size, color-blind safe signals
- [ ] Options for screen shake, flashes and motion
- [ ] Difficulty or assist options

## Quality

- [ ] A test plan per build; bugs have steps, severity and an owner
- [ ] Crash and save-data tests; play on every target device
- [ ] Outside playtests at alpha and beta, with notes turned into tasks

## Store submission

- [ ] **itch.io**: the itch zip from Publish uploaded as an HTML game; page with cover, screenshots, controls and credits
- [ ] **Google Play**: a Play developer account; the release's `app.aab` signed with your own key (added as secrets in your GitHub project); name, description, two or more screenshots, icon, privacy answers, age rating
- [ ] **iPhone (TestFlight)**: needs a Mac and a paid Apple developer account; Publish prepares the build file, you upload and invite testers
- [ ] **Computer app**: installers for Windows, Mac and Linux are unsigned; say so on the download page, or sign them yourself
- [ ] Each store's rules read; test builds sent early; time allowed for a rejected first try
- [ ] Launch day plan, a patch plan, and a way for players to report problems

## Team roles

Director, Producer, Design, Programming, Art, Audio, QA, Release. Write down who decides what.

paths.title: Make a website: Basics
paths.summary: You can go from nothing to a page people can open in one sitting. You do not need an AI or any code.
paths.body:
# Make a website: Basics

You can go from nothing to a page people can open in one sitting. You do not need an AI or any code.

## The short version

1. **Say what it is for.** One sentence in the project's vision: who the site is for and what they should do there.
2. **Pick a template.** Open **Design**, choose **Website**, and pick the template closest to what you want. Link page, portfolio, shop, blog, cafe, band and more are there.
3. **Change the words and pictures.** Click any text to type over it. Click a picture to swap it. Pick a look (colors and fonts) from the side.
4. **Check it.** Press **Check my site**. It lists what to fix in plain words, such as a missing title or a picture with no description.
5. **Publish.** Press **Publish**. A safety check runs first, then you get a play link and a QR code. Under **Where it goes** you can also **Download it** as a zip, or make **A link that stays up** with your own GitHub sign-in.
6. **Share.** Send the link. Anyone can open it on a phone or computer, with no account.

## Good first choices

- Start with one page. A second page can wait.
- Write the headline for a stranger: what this is, in eight words or fewer.
- Use your own photos where you can. They beat stock pictures.
- Put one clear button near the top: Book, Buy, Join or Contact.

## If you get lost

Press **?** and pick **What should I do next?** It looks at your project and gives you one step. Or ask Flint: "make a website for my bakery".

paths.title: Make a website: In practice
paths.summary: The site works. Now make it good for real visitors.
paths.body:
# Make a website: In practice

The site works. Now make it good for real visitors.

## Structure

- **One job per page.** Home says what you do. Other pages answer one question each: prices, work, about, contact.
- **Keep the menu to five links or fewer.** Everything else goes in the footer.
- **Write the first screen last.** Once the rest is written, you know what the headline should promise.

## Words

- Short sentences. Say "you" more than "we".
- Every section ends with something to do: a button or a link.
- Read it out loud once. Fix what you trip on.

## Pictures

- Crop to the subject. Wide banners for the top, squares for grids.
- Give every picture a description. Check my site flags the ones without.
- Keep each picture small enough to load fast on a phone (see Production for sizes).

## Working with others

- Invite a friend with one link and edit together, live.
- Leave comments on the page itself, so the note sits next to the thing it is about.
- Put each change on the **Task Board** so nothing is lost: one task, one owner, one next button.

## Before each publish

1. Open the preview at phone size and scroll the whole page.
2. Tap every button and link.
3. Run **Check my site** and clear the list.
4. Publish. Each publish is a new version, and you can go back to an older one.

## Where it can go

Publish has a **Where it goes** list. It checks the project first, then offers what fits:

- **Play link**: works right away while the tribe's computer is on.
- **Download it**: a zip of the finished page, for any web service you already use.
- **A link that stays up**: a lasting address through your own GitHub sign-in, updated on every publish.
- **Install on phones**: adds an icon and an offline copy, once it has a link that stays up.

The play link is for trying things. Use the lasting link for anything you print or post.

paths.title: Make a website: Production
paths.summary: A checklist for sites that carry real traffic, a brand or sales. Copy it into a doc and tick it off per release.
paths.body:
# Make a website: Production

A checklist for sites that carry real traffic, a brand or sales. Copy it into a doc and tick it off per release.

## Content and structure

- [ ] Every page has a unique title (under 60 characters) and a description (under 160)
- [ ] One H1 per page, headings in order, no skipped levels
- [ ] A share picture (1200 x 630) and a favicon are set
- [ ] A custom "not found" page links back home
- [ ] Privacy and terms pages exist if you collect anything

## Performance budget

- [ ] First screen under 200 KB of pictures; whole page under 1.5 MB
- [ ] Pictures sized to their slot, saved as WebP or AVIF, lazy loaded below the first screen
- [ ] No more than two font families, four weights in total
- [ ] Largest element on screen in under 2.5 seconds on a mid-range phone
- [ ] Layout does not jump while loading (set width and height on pictures)

## Accessibility

- [ ] Text contrast of at least 4.5 to 1 (3 to 1 for large text)
- [ ] Every picture has a description, or is marked as decoration
- [ ] Everything works with the keyboard alone, with a visible focus ring
- [ ] Tap targets at least 44 px; forms have labels and clear errors
- [ ] Motion respects the "reduce motion" setting

## Release pipeline

- [ ] Changes are tasks with an owner and a reviewer
- [ ] Review on the preview at 390, 768 and 1280 px wide
- [ ] Check my site is clean; Publish's safety check passes
- [ ] Version noted with what changed; the last good version is known for rollback
- [ ] Links, forms and the buy flow tested on the live link after publishing

## Where it goes

- [ ] Public traffic uses **A link that stays up**, not the play link
- [ ] **Download it** kept as a zip per release, as a backup and for your own web service
- [ ] **Install on phones** on, with name, icon and offline copy checked on a real phone
- [ ] The GitHub sign-in used for publishing belongs to the owner, not to a helper

## Roles

Owner (decides), Writer, Designer, Builder, Reviewer. One person can hold several, but the reviewer should not be the builder.
